title: Comparative Risk of Atrial Fibrillation Onset in Statin‐Treated Patients Initiating Icosapent Ethyl and Omega‐3 Acid Ethyl Esters: A Retrospective Cohort Study
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.abstract:
Icosapent ethyl (IPE) and omega‐3‐acid ethyl esters (docosahexaenoic acid [DHA]/eicosapentaenoic acid [EPA]) are approved as adjunct therapies to statins for reducing cardiovascular events in at‐risk patients. However, concerns remain regarding a potential link between IPE and atrial fibrillation (AF). We compared the risk of AF onset in patients who initiated IPE versus DHA/EPA as adjuncts to statin therapy.

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Merative MarketScan Commercial Claims and Medicare Supplemental database in the United States. An active‐comparator, new‐user study design was applied. Adults diagnosed with dyslipidemia and receiving statin therapy who initiated IPE or DHA/EPA between January 2013 and June 2021 were identified. A propensity score–matched cohort was created using baseline demographic characteristics, comorbidities, and medication dispensing records, with exact matching on therapy initiation period. Patients were followed for up to 2 years while they were on IPE or DHA/EPA therapy to identify incident AF. Cumulative incidence was estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods, and risks between groups were compared using Cox proportional hazards analysis.

The propensity score–matched cohort included 17 635 participants, with a mean age of 55 years, and was predominantly men (65.4%). Over 2 years, the cumulative incidence of AF from IPE and DHA/EPA was 5.20% (95% CI, 4.62%–5.84%) and 4.07% (95% CI, 3.58%–4.62%) respectively, resulting in a hazard ratio of 1.21 (95% CI, 1.03–1.42).

These findings suggest that, in adult patients who are AF naïve, IPE may be associated with a higher risk of AF compared with DHA/EPA when used as add‐on therapy with statins.
sections.methods:
We conducted a retrospective cohort study and applied an active‐comparator, new‐user design. Data from the Merative MarketScan Commercial Claims and Medicare Supplemental Databases, covering January 2013 to December 2021, were used for this study. These are large administrative health care claims databases in the United States that capture medical and outpatient pharmacy claims for patients covered by employer‐sponsored insurance plans.

The University of Illinois Chicago Institutional Review Board deemed the use of the database for this study exempt from review. The study was reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines. 8 Data from this study are available upon request from the corresponding authors.

The target population for this study were patients who have dyslipidemia and are on statin therapy. Using National Drug Codes from outpatient dispensing records, we identified adults (≥18 years) who initiated either IPE or DHA/EPA between January 2013 and June 2021. The date of the first IPE or DHA/EPA dispensing was defined as the index date for this study. To be eligible, patients were required to have a dispensing of statin on the index date or to have an active supply of statin based on the most recent dispensing record before the index date.

To ensure that patients were new users of the therapies of interest, we required continuous enrollment in the database for 365 days before the index date. Individuals with a diagnosis of AF during this baseline period were excluded from the study. AF was identified using diagnosis codes: International Classification of Diseases , Ninth Revision ( ICD‐9 ) 427.31, and Tenth Revision ( ICD‐10 ) 148.0, 148.1, 148.2, and 148.91. We also excluded patients who were diagnosed with AF within the first 30 days after IPE or DHA/EPA initiation, during which the risk carried over from the baseline period could outweigh the effect caused by the IPE or DHA/EPA use.

Patient characteristics of interest included demographic and clinical factors, with clinical factors covering both comorbidities and medication history. Demographic information included age, sex, region, and year of IPE or DHA/EPA initiation. We identified comorbidities from baseline inpatient and outpatient diagnosis records using ICD‐9 and ICD‐10 codes. For this, all available inpatient and outpatient encounters before the index date were used. Baseline comorbid conditions identified included acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina, non–ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction, and ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction), heart failure (unspecified, systolic, and diastolic), diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and hyperthyroidism. Baseline use of medications was identified using National Drug Codes from the outpatient pharmacy claims in the year preceding the index date. Medications included angiotensin II receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors, glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists, sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 inhibitors, biguanides, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 inhibitors, and insulin.

Propensity scores (PSs) were calculated using logistic regression based on the demographic and clinical characteristics, excluding treatment year. The model estimated the odds of receiving IPE treatment given the other covariates. Comparable groups were then created using PS matching (nearest‐neighbor matching with a caliper of 0.1 times the pooled SD of the logit of the PS), along with exact matching on the index year (categorized into 3 groups: 2013–2015, 2016–2018, and 2019–2021). This approach accounted for shifts in prescribing patterns over time, with IPE use gradually increasing following its approval and DHA/EPA use declining. The standardized mean difference for each variable was used as a balance diagnostic in the matched cohort.

Individuals were followed for up to 2 years. The primary outcome was the incidence of AF within 2 years of initiating IPE or DHA/EPA. A health care claim for AF in either an inpatient or outpatient setting defined by the diagnosis code of AF at any position in a claim was considered as the outcome. Censoring from the follow‐up occurred when the participant met any of the following criteria, whichever happened first: treatment discontinuation (defined as a gap of supply of >30 days), switching treatments, disenrollment from the database before end of 2‐year follow‐up, or at the end of the study. Any discontinuation of the treatments of interest or statins was considered a treatment discontinuation. For example, if there was a continuous supply of IPE or DHA/EPA but a gap of >30 days in statin supply, follow‐up was discontinued and the observation was censored.

We assessed the cumulative incidence of AF onset in both treatment groups using Kaplan–Meier estimates. Comparative analysis was performed using a Cox proportional hazards regression model to estimate HRs and 95% CIs for AF onset associated with IPE versus DHA/EPA. To account for the potential for different baseline hazard functions across subgroups, we also performed a stratified Cox proportional hazards regression model, using PS matched‐pair identifiers as strata. Subgroup analyses were conducted on the basis of age (<65 and ≥65 years), sex, and the presence or absence of comorbidities to assess the consistency of the association across the various subgroups. Each analysis was performed on a separate PS‐matched cohort, with exact matching on treatment initiation period. In each case, all previously described confounding factors, excluding the subgroup‐defining variable, were included in the PS model.
sections.results:
We identified 262 961 adult individuals who initiated treatment with either IPE or DHA/EPA between January 1, 2013, and June 30, 2021, of whom 149 004 met the 1‐year continuous baseline enrollment criteria. Among these patients, 67 285 were on statin therapy at the time of IPE or DHA/EPA initiation. After excluding 2966 individuals who had a diagnosis of AF before initiating IPE or DHA/EPA and removing patients who were censored or had an AF event within the first 30 days, a total of 62 609 patients remained in the cohort, of whom 31 133 were in the IPE group and 31 476 in the DHA/EPA group (Figure 1 ).

DHA indicates docosahexaenoic acid; EPA, eicosapentaenoic acid; IPE, icosapent ethyl; and PS, propensity score.

The baseline characteristics of the 2 groups before PS matching are shown in Table 1 . The age distribution differed between the groups. Specifically, the proportion of patients aged ≥65 years were higher in the DHA/EPA group (16.8%) compared with the IPE‐initiating group (12.6%). Conversely, the IPE‐treated group has more patients aged 55 to 64 years (42.9%) compared with the DHA/EPA group (39.8%). The proportion of male patients was higher in the IPE group (67.9%) compared with the DHA/EPA group (62.1%). There was a clear time trend in the use of both treatments. Among those who initiated DHA/EPA, the majority did so in 2013 to 2015 (55.8%), with fewer initiating in 2016 to 2018 (29.5%) and 2019 to 2021 (14.7%). In contrast, among those who initiated IPE, 16.9% did so in 2013 to 2015, 26.1% in 2016 to 2018, and the majority (56.9%) in 2019 to 2021. There were notable differences in medication use between the IPE and DHA/EPA treatment groups. Medications more commonly used in the IPE group included angiotensin II receptor blockers (30.1% versus 26.0%), angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors (0.4% versus 0.1%), β blockers (37.2% versus 33.8%), glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists (14.3% versus 6.8%), sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 inhibitors (16.8% versus 6.2%), biguanides (39.4% versus 34.5%), thiazolidinediones (3.5% versus 2.9%), dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 inhibitors (11.6% versus 10.8%), insulin (14.6% versus 12.7%), and calcium channel blockers (21.7% versus 21.1%). In contrast, medications more commonly used in the DHA/EPA group included angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors (33.7% versus 32.6%) and sulfonylureas (12.8% versus 11.7%).

In this matched cohort, there were 17 635 individuals in each group, and the demographic and clinical characteristics were well balanced between the 2 groups. The matched cohort had a median age of 55 (interquartile range, 49–61) years, and 65.4% of them were men. Among medication classes included in the analysis, the commonly used medications were biguanides (37.0%), β blockers (34.1%), angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors (32.6%), angiotensin II receptor blockers (28.4%), and calcium channel blockers (21.8%). Among the comorbidities measured, there was a high prevalence of hypertension (39.0%) and type 2 diabetes (28.1%) (Table 2) .

During the follow‐up, there were 330 AF events in the IPE group compared with 281 in the DHA/EPA group. The Kaplan–Meier estimates from the matched cohort indicated that the cumulative incidence of AF at 1 year was 1.68% (95% CI, 1.44–1.96%) for IPE users and 1.48% (95% CI, 1.26–1.74%) for DHA/EPA users (Figure 2 ). At 2 years, the cumulative incidence was 5.20% (95% CI, 4.62%–5.84%) and 4.07% (95% CI, 3.58%–4.62%), respectively. The 2‐year HR for AF was 1.21 (95% CI, 1.03–1.42) as estimated by the Cox proportional hazards regression model. A stratified Cox regression model accounting for the matched pairs produced the same point estimate, with a 95% CI of 0.96 to 1.52, reflecting reduced precision but consistent direction and magnitude of effect (Table 3) .

The results of the subgroup analyses are presented in Figure S1 . The findings of the primary analysis were generally consistent across most subgroups, with HRs indicating an increased risk of AF among IPE users. However, most of these associations were not statistically significant, likely due to the small number of events within individual subgroups. In a few subgroups, such as patients with unstable angina, non–ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction, a history of diastolic heart failure, type 1 or type 2 diabetes, and a history of anxiety, the HRs suggested a reduced risk of AF among IPE users. None of these associations were statistically significant.
sections.discussion:
Our findings suggest that among statin users, the initiation of IPE compared to DHA/EPA is associated with a higher risk of AF over a 2‐year period. Subgroup analyses generally supported the primary results, although most associations were not statistically significant. Past studies have shown varying risks of AF associated with different omega‐3 fatty acid formulations. The REDUCE‐IT trial, which evaluated IPE at a dose of 4 g daily in patients with established cardiovascular disease or diabetes, and additional risk factors, reported a higher incidence of AF or flutter in the IPE group compared with placebo (5.3% versus 3.9%; P =0.003), and also a greater rate of AF‐related hospitalizations (3.1% versus 2.1%; P =0.004). 2 Although our study used a different comparator (DHA/EPA) instead of placebo, we observed a similarly increased incidence of AF in the IPE‐treated group, consistent with findings from REDUCE‐IT. Given that our study population was younger than that of the REDUCE‐IT trial, our findings indicate the risk of IPE‐associated AF to a broader population, including individuals who may be at comparatively lower risk of cardiovascular events than those typically enrolled in clinical trials but are taking IPE for its protective benefits.

Though there is no direct comparison of AF risk between IPE and DHA/EPA, other trials have investigated the risk of AF associated with different omega‐3 formulations containing both DHA and EPA. The STRENGTH (A Long‐Term Outcomes Study to Assess Statin Residual Risk Reduction With Epanova in High Cardiovascular Risk Patients With Hypertriglyceridemia) trial studying omega‐3 carboxylic acids (another combination of DHA and EPA) at 4 g daily in high‐risk patients found no significant cardiovascular benefit but reported an increased risk of AF in the omega‐3 carboxylic acids group compared with placebo (2.2% versus 1.3%; P <0.001). 9 The OMEMI (Omega‐3 Fatty Acids in Elderly With Myocardial Infarction) trial, which evaluated n‐3 polyunsaturated fatty acids compared to placebo in older patients following a recent acute myocardial infarction, found no significant reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events. However, the study result showed a higher incidence of AF in the n‐3 polyunsaturated fatty acids treated group, although this difference did not reach statistical significance. 10 In an observational study (MESA [Multi‐Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis]) on individuals without cardiovascular disease, higher plasma levels of DHA (but not EPA only or EPA in combination with DHA) were associated with a lower risk of incident AF. 11 A recent systematic review and meta‐analysis of 7 large cardiovascular RCTs found the use of marine omega‐3 fatty acid supplementation increased the risk of AF by 1.25 times (95% CI, 1.07–1.46), with an increase in HR for high‐dose omega‐3 fatty acids. 12 Though none of these studies attempted to measure the comparative risk of IPE versus DHA/EPA as we did in our study, this body of evidence shows that there are concerns about AF not only with IPE but also with different types of omega‐3 products. The MESA study suggested a potentially protective effect of DHA, lending support to the hypothesis that DHA may mitigate AF risk. These studies also highlight a potential dose–response effect, which could be related to an imbalance between DHA and EPA or to the high amount of EPA present in IPE therapy. Nevertheless, these findings require further clarification, and future studies are needed to assess any causal association between EPA and AF, as well as to determine whether a dose–response relationship exists.

Despite the mechanisms by which omega‐3 fatty acids may influence the risk of AF are not fully understood, emerging evidence has begun to postulate several potential electrophysiological and structural pathways. Traditionally, omega‐3 fatty acids have been known to stabilize cardiac cell membranes and protect against arrhythmias (particularly ventricular arrhythmias) through their direct electrophysiological effects and modulation of processes involved in atrial remodeling. 13 However, omega‐3 fatty acids also directly influence cardiac ion channels, including those regulating calcium, sodium, and potassium currents. These interactions can affect the duration of the ventricular action potential and potentially disrupt the heart's electrical stability. 13 , 14 Therefore, though omega‐3 fatty acids may reduce arrhythmias in situations involving triggered activity, under some conditions they can also contribute to the development of reentrant arrhythmias. 13 , 14 , 15 This potential dual action could account for the conflicting results seen in clinical trials on fish oil consumption and its association with sudden death and arrhythmias. 15 Emerging studies suggest that these effects might be mediated, at least in part, by a mechanosensitive ion channel protein (PIEZO), which are mechanosensitive ion channels that respond to physical forces. 14 When mechanical stress increases, the dome‐shaped structure of these channels flattens, opening a central pore and allowing positively charged ions like calcium to flow into the cell. 13 Omega‐3 fatty acids, which are incorporated into the cardiomyocyte surface membranes, may influence this mechanical sensitivity by making the membranes thinner and more compliant. 13 The specific effects of omega‐3 fatty acids on PIEZO1 activity appear to depend on the type of fatty acid. DHA prolongs the active state of PIEZO1 channels, while EPA causes them to deactivate more quickly. Thus, the ratio of DHA and EPA in omega‐3 fatty acids could be a critical determinant of PIEZO1‐mediated effects. The imbalance and increased ratio of DHA can lead to AF. 13 , 16 Similarly, since IPE consists solely of EPA, any potential association between IPE intake, alterations in the DHA:EPA ratio, and increased AF risk remains speculative and warrants further investigation. PIEZO1 channels may also be involved in mechanical stress signaling in other atrial cell types, such as fibroblasts. Research shows that PIEZO1 expression and activity are increased in atrial fibroblasts. 14 , 16 Moreover, changes to the cell membrane caused by omega‐3 fatty acid intake may affect more than just PIEZO1 channels. These alterations could influence voltage‐gated ion channels, ionic pumps, cell surface receptors, and interactions between the extracellular matrix and the cytoskeleton, all of which may contribute to a proarrhythmic environment. 14 Further clinical trials are required to understand the processes by which omega‐3 fatty acid supplementation increases the AF risk and alters the electrophysiological characteristics of the myocardium.

Although recent guidelines recommend IPE for its cardiovascular benefits, 1 , 2 our findings suggest that it should be used carefully due to the associated risk of AF. This highlights the importance of balancing therapeutic benefits with arrhythmia risks on the basis of patients' underlying health status and the need for individualized risk assessment. As IPE use has been increasing, our results and emerging clinical evidence underscore the need for evaluation of AF risk in IPE and other omega‐3 fatty acid therapies. Particular attention should be given to the DHA:EPA ratio, patient‐specific risk profiles, and long‐term AF monitoring.

Our study has several limitations that should be considered. First, we were unable to capture the dispensing of over‐the‐counter (OTC) fish oils. However, it is unlikely that patients would concurrently take IPE or DHA/EPA together with OTC fish oils. Even with a small chance of concurrent use of prescription IPE or DHA/EPA with nutritional supplements, the pattern of the OTC medication or dietary supplement use would not be different between the IPE‐ and DHA/EPA‐treated groups, having no or very nominal influence on the exposure–outcome association. Additionally, lifestyle factors such as dietary omega‐3 fatty acid intake, smoking, and alcohol use are potential confounders that could impact the risk of AF but are not captured or are incompletely recorded in the available data set. In particular, dietary omega‐3 intake may introduce unmeasured confounding, as we could not adjust for individual dietary habits that may influence cardiovascular outcomes.

We also did not account for changes in statin dosage or the alteration of other medications after the follow‐up period began. While we believe that our matching strategy reduced the concern on the difference in the patterns of the use of the other agents or statin dose alterations between the IPE‐ and DHA/EPA‐treated groups, future research could benefit from clinical trials that more rigorously control these factors. We did not follow‐up on participant AF outcomes in this study. Understanding of the consequences of AF, including the need for therapeutic interventions, the potential progression to paroxysmal or permanent AF, and associated health care costs, is important for patients considering the use of these agents or dietary supplements. Additionally, the effects among patients who discontinue IPE or DHA/EPA, including whether AF events persist after discontinuation, should be further explored in future studies.

The interpretation of our findings should be accompanied by understanding the inability to clearly determine whether the incidence of AF is driven by high concentrations of EPA, which may promote AF, or by absence of DHA, which may have protective effects against AF. Furthermore, we compared AF incidence to a treatment group with a potential AF risk, rather than to an untreated control group. This decision was made because, in an untreated group, we cannot be certain that patients have not taken OTC fish oils, which could introduce differential misclassification. Additionally, matching with an untreated group is not methodologically justified, as it would likely introduce confounding by disease severity or confounding by indication. Conducting such a comparison within an observational study using administrative data in the United States presents challenges, as OTC fish oil use is difficult to verify. Addressing this limitation would require well‐monitored, randomized trials to ensure accurate classification of omega‐3 exposure.

Various methodological concerns warrant additional data integration for future analysis. For example, we did not have access to laboratory data, including lipid profiles, which limits our ability to confirm guideline‐adherent prescribing, assess potential lipid level‐related confounding factors, or determine if changes in AF incidence may be linked to lipid levels. Residual confounding can be addressed by incorporating laboratory test results into PS matching or regression‐based adjustment. Additionally, if the data could be linked with individual‐level death records, competing risks analysis that accounts for death as a competing event should be considered to derive a more accurate estimate of the association between exposure to IPE and the onset of AF.

sections.conclusion: In this large real‐world cohort study of statin users, initiation of IPE was associated with a higher risk of AF compared with DHA/EPA over a 2‐year follow‐up period. These findings highlight potential safety differences between omega‐3 formulations and underscore the importance of individualized risk–benefit assessment when selecting add‐on lipid‐lowering therapies. Further research is needed to clarify the mechanisms underlying these associations and to determine whether specific patient populations may be at greater risk.
